passage:
Saptami afternoon. On the roof, Preeti points at a cloud. "A dragon! With a curly tail!" Bidisha didi squints and laughs. "It's eating the pandal!"
Ashtami night. The pandal lights throw a spiky shadow on the bedroom wall. Preeti pulls the sheet over her head. "Monster," she whispers. Didi holds her hand and flaps the curtain. The monster wobbles and turns back into a curtain.
Navami morning. Preeti makes a shadow bunny on the wall with her own fingers, giggling. "Didi, look! Mine!"

qa.q: What did Preeti see in the cloud on Saptami?
qa.a: A dragon with a curly tail.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel about the spiky shadow on Ashtami night?
qa.a: She felt frightened, pulling the sheet over her head and whispering "Monster", although it was only the pandal lights on the curtain.

qa.q: What helped Preeti with the shadow, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha didi held her hand and flapped the curtain so the monster wobbled back into a curtain, letting Preeti see where the shape came from.

qa.q: What would change if Bidisha had said "Don't be silly, go to sleep"?
qa.a: Preeti might have stayed scared of the wall in the dark, and might not have found out on Navami that she could make shadow shapes herself.

grounding: A child finds a dragon in a cloud and a monster in a night shadow, delight and fear coming from the same shape-finding.

passage:
The winter fog had not lifted by seven, and Sahil's blue away jersey hung on the balcony line, still damp. The inter-school final was at nine.
"Just wear the new one," Mummy said.
"This is the one I wore when we beat Green Valley," Sahil said, already plugging in the iron. "And in the semi. And the quarter." He did not mention the league match they had lost 0-3 in it, back in August, rain lashing the ground.
Steam hissed off the cloth. The school bus honked twice at the gate. Abhinav called his phone: "Where are you? Everyone's on!"
"Two minutes!" Sahil pulled on the warm, half-dry shirt and ran, sure that everything would be fine now.

qa.q: At what time was the inter-school final?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: Why does Sahil risk missing the bus to iron the damp jersey?
qa.a: He feels anxious without it and sure it brings wins, linking it to three victories while forgetting the 0-3 loss he also played in it.

qa.q: What could Sahil try, to check whether the shirt really matters?
qa.a: He could list every match he wore it in, wins and losses, and notice it was there for the 0-3 defeat too, so the wins may come from how the team played.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel waiting on the bus?
qa.a: Abhinav is probably impatient and worried that the team will be late or a player short before a final.

grounding: A teenager insists on the jersey worn in past wins, reading a link between the shirt and the results.

passage:
On the night of Sao Joao, with plastic hammers squeaking all over Porto, Paulo grabbed Soo-ah's arm. "Look. 11:11 again."
She glanced at the church clock. "So?"
"So it's the fourth time this week. And my new bus is the 111. And my flatmate's birthday is November eleventh. That's not random, Soo-ah. Something's lining up." His eyes were bright, almost proud, as if he had been let in on a secret nobody else had spotted.
"How many times did you look at a clock and it wasn't 11:11?" she asked.
Paulo waved the question away. "You wouldn't get it." He took a photo of the clock face and saved it to a folder he had named Signs.
Behind them, a stranger bopped someone on the head with a hammer, laughing.

qa.q: What had Paulo named the folder for the photo?
qa.a: Signs.

qa.q: How does Paulo feel about noticing all the elevens?
qa.a: He feels excited and a bit proud, as if he alone has spotted a hidden pattern, so he brushes off Soo-ah's question.

qa.q: What would you advise Paulo to do with the pattern?
qa.a: Test it, as Soo-ah hinted: for a week, note every time he checks a clock, not only the 11:11s, and see whether the elevens still stand out.

qa.q: Why might Soo-ah react differently to the 11:11s?
qa.a: Soo-ah thinks about all the times Paulo looked and saw other numbers, so the sign looks more like a chance streak than a plan.

grounding: A young adult links unrelated elevens into a secret pattern and feels special for having noticed it.

subtype: Testing the pattern before believing it [Response]
passage:
For two weeks Zubin had been seeing R and K everywhere: on auto number plates in Andheri, on a cafe receipt, on a shop sign near the station. Rukhsana Kapoor had moved to Pune a month ago. It felt as if the city was sending messages.
On Saturday he sat with Ganga at the bus stop and tried something new. "If this were pure chance, how often would I see an R or a K?" He counted the next fifty number plates. Fourteen had one.
"That's... just normal," he said slowly.
Ganga nodded. "And you've been looking for them."
He admitted the searching had been keeping him awake, heart racing, till two most nights. That evening he booked a session with a counsellor through his office. Walking home, he saw a K on a truck and let it pass.

qa.q: How many of the fifty number plates had an R or a K?
qa.a: Fourteen had one.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when the count came out at fourteen?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a little relieved, saying slowly "That's... just normal", as the messages began to look like chance.

qa.q: Which of Zubin's steps would you advise someone else to copy?
qa.a: Asking how the pattern would look by pure chance and testing it on new plates, and, since the searching kept him awake, booking a counsellor as he did.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel watching Zubin count the number plates?
qa.a: Ganga probably feels concerned but hopeful, gently pointing out "you've been looking for them" and glad to see Zubin test the idea.

grounding: An adult tests a letter pattern against chance on fresh number plates and books a counsellor when the searching overwhelms him.

subtype: Glee when the sibling is scolded [Actor]
passage:
On Holi morning Mummy had already told Yash off twice, once for spilt gulal and once for the water balloon on the TV. Now it was Manjula's turn. She had sprayed pink right across Dadi's white sari.
"Manjula! What did I just say?" Mummy's voice went sharp.
Yash, behind the sofa, felt a smile creep up. Didi was in trouble too. He pressed his lips together, but the corners twitched.
Then Manjula's chin wobbled. Yash looked down at his purple fingers and suddenly didn't want the smile any more.

qa.q: What did Manjula spray pink?
qa.a: Dadi's white sari.

qa.q: Why does Yash smile when Manjula is scolded, and how does that change?
qa.a: He feels pleased that Didi is in trouble too after his own two scoldings, as if things are even, but when her chin wobbles he feels guilty and looks away.

qa.q: How could Mummy help both children after this?
qa.a: She could talk calmly with each of them later, and ask Yash how it felt to be scolded and then to see Didi scolded, so he can name the mixed feeling.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula at that moment?
qa.a: Manjula feels upset and embarrassed, her chin wobbling at Mummy's sharp voice while her little brother watches from behind the sofa.

grounding: A young child smirks when his sister is told off after his own scoldings, then looks away guilty.

subtype: Rival's failure feels good and bad [Actor]
passage:
Choir notes, 12 December, Christmas concert solo auditions
Charu went fourth. Before it, she told the whole line she would "obviously" get the solo. Her voice cracked on the high note of the second verse, twice, and she walked off red-faced.
Mohit was next. For a second he grinned, quick and bright, and nudged the boy beside him. Then he saw Charu wiping her eyes by the piano, and the grin vanished. He stared at the floor through his own audition; the notes were right but the feeling was flat.
Afterwards he stayed back. "I was happy when she cracked. Is that horrible?"
I told him the flash was human, and that what he does next matters more. He decided to tell Charu her first verse was lovely. I will check in with both of them on Monday.

qa.q: On which note did Charu's voice crack?
qa.a: On the high note of the second verse, twice.

qa.q: What did Mohit feel when Charu's voice cracked, and how did it change?
qa.a: He felt a quick flash of glee at the boastful rival failing, then shame when he saw her wiping her eyes, which is why he asks if it was horrible.

qa.q: What could Mohit do next with the mixed feeling?
qa.a: As he decided, tell Charu her first verse was lovely, and quietly think about why her boasting stung him so much.

qa.q: How might Charu feel if she had noticed Mohit's grin?
qa.a: She would likely feel even more humiliated and alone, as if her failure were a joke to the others in line.

grounding: A teacher's note records a teenager's grin at a boastful rival's failed audition turning quickly to shame.

subtype: Friend notices glee at another's downfall [Observer]
passage:
Twelve minutes before the next lecture, the engineering canteen was packed and deafening. Jatin squeezed onto the bench beside Mohit, who was scrolling the class group.
"Look," Mohit murmured, tilting the screen. Farah, the batch topper, had posted the wrong answer key for the circuits quiz, and three people had already corrected her. Mohit's mouth twitched. "Miss Perfect, finally."
Jatin could have laughed along; two others at the table did. Instead he waited until they got up, the crowd pushing them toward the stairs.
"You've been riding on her since the internship list came out," Jatin said quietly. "Is this about that?"
Mohit was silent for a whole flight of stairs. "Maybe," he said. "She got it. I didn't."

qa.q: What had Farah posted in the class group?
qa.a: The wrong answer key for the circuits quiz.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling when two others laughed along?
qa.a: Jatin likely felt uneasy and torn, not wanting to mock Farah or shame Mohit in front of the table, so he waited for a quieter moment.

qa.q: What worked about the way Jatin raised it?
qa.a: He spoke privately and asked a question, "Is this about that?", instead of scolding, which let Mohit admit the envy about the internship.

qa.q: What is it like for Mohit to hear Jatin's question?
qa.a: Mohit is caught off guard and silent for a flight of stairs, then admits "She got it. I didn't," which suggests some relief at naming the hurt behind the glee.

grounding: A friend notices a classmate enjoying the top student's slip and quietly asks what the envy is about instead of joining in.

passage:
The office Diwali lunch was all fairy lights and kaju katli, and everyone knew by now that Eshaan's delivery pilot in Noida had been shut down after six weeks.
"Tough luck, man," said Tenzin, patting his shoulder. "These things happen." But as Eshaan turned, he caught Tenzin glancing at someone from sales, and the two of them sharing a small, tight smile.
Eshaan filled his plate and found he wasn't hungry. Every "so sorry, yaar" now seemed to have a second voice underneath. The pilot had been his first big idea, the one he had pitched so loudly in March.
He carried his plate to the empty pantry and ate standing by the window, the laughter from the hall sounding very far away.

qa.q: How long had the delivery pilot run before it was shut down?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What is Eshaan feeling as he eats alone in the pantry?
qa.a: He feels lonely and small, as if colleagues are quietly enjoying his failure, so even the kind words seem to hide a second voice.

qa.q: What small step could help Eshaan after the lunch?
qa.a: He could talk to one colleague he trusts about how the shutdown felt, and remind himself that pitching a bold idea took courage, whatever others think.

qa.q: What would change if Tenzin's words had come without the glance and smile?
qa.a: Eshaan might have felt supported rather than mocked, and could have stayed in the hall instead of retreating to the pantry.

grounding: A colleague whose project failed senses smiles behind polite sympathy at a Diwali lunch and feels lonely and small.

subtype: Noticing the pleasure without acting on it [Response]
passage:
The shutter of Eshaan's new mobile-repair shop in Rampur bazaar stayed down for the third morning, a hand-written board taped to it: Closed till further notice. Vinita, unlocking her tailoring shop opposite, felt a quick, warm flicker. He had laughed at her old sewing machine last Diwali.
She typed to her cousin, "Guess whose big shop just shut," and stopped. Deleted it.
Threading a needle, she asked herself why it felt so good. The answer came uncomfortably fast: she had wanted a bigger shop herself and never dared to try.
At noon she saw Eshaan sitting on his step, staring at nothing. She poured two cups of tea from her flask and crossed the road. "Sit inside for a bit," she said. "It's hot out here."

qa.q: What was written on the board taped to Eshaan's shutter?
qa.a: Closed till further notice.

qa.q: Why does Vinita delete the message to her cousin?
qa.a: She notices the warm flicker of glee, feels uneasy about it, and does not want to spread Eshaan's trouble just to enjoy it.

qa.q: What does Vinita's question to herself help her see?
qa.a: Asking why it felt good shows her that the envy points to her own wish for a bigger shop, something she can act on for herself.

qa.q: What might the cup of tea mean to Eshaan, sitting on his step?
qa.a: For Eshaan, alone after the shop closed, tea from someone he once laughed at might feel comforting and a little humbling.

grounding: An adult notices glee at a neighbour's shop closing, keeps it to herself, reflects on her envy and offers kindness.

passage: Last Saraswati Puja our para had a drawing contest, and I, Irawati, was sure my peacock would win. Arnab drew the river behind his house, with a boat and a tiny dog on the bank. When they called his name for first prize, I clapped so hard my palms stung. I even whistled, which Ma says is rude. Arnab looked back at me and grinned, holding his certificate as if it might fly away. I was so happy for him. But on the walk home, a small part of me kept thinking about my peacock. Both feelings were there together, like two sweets in one box.

qa.q: What did Arnab draw?
qa.a: The river behind his house, with a boat and a tiny dog on the bank.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling during the prize announcement and on the walk home?
qa.a: Irawati felt real joy for Arnab, clapping till the palms stung, and later a small pang of disappointment about the peacock.

qa.q: What would you tell Irawati about having both feelings?
qa.a: That it is normal to be happy for a friend and still wish you had won; the pang can even become a goal for next year's contest.

qa.q: How did Arnab seem to take Irawati's loud clapping?
qa.a: Arnab looked back and grinned, so the cheering likely made him feel proud and supported by a friend.

grounding: A child cheers a friend's prize with warmth while a small pang of wanting to win sits underneath.
